state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you walk me through how changing all the plants by the same proportion would affect the range in this case?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, so I think the range is the difference between the tallest and shortest plants, right? If I cut all the heights in half, the tallest and shortest would also be halved, but I guess they would still have the same difference. But with Katie's idea, if we add 3 cm to each plant, wouldn't that change the difference too? I'm not really sure how to figure that out. Can you help me understand it better?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of a similar situation where changing all values by the same amount would actually change the range?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess if I think about it, if I had a set of numbers like \( 1, 2, 3 \) and then added \( 5 \) to each, they would become \( 6, 7, 8 \). The tallest and shortest would still be \( 8 \) and \( 6 \), so the range would change, right? But I'm still confused about how cutting them in half keeps the range the same. Can you explain that part again?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher's Turn 3 question asks the student to find a counterexample that would actually reinforce rather than correct the misconception, and the student's final turn shows they remain confused, believing adding constants changes the range while halving keeps it the same (the opposite of reality).
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher uses questions rather than direct answers, Turn 3 asks the student to find a counterexample to their own correct reasoning (which would confuse rather than guide them), and the teacher fails to use probing questions to help the student recognize their error in Turn 4 where they incorrectly conclude that adding 5 to each number changes the range.
